title: מַסֶּכֶת אָבוֹת — פֶּרֶק שֵׁנִי
part: Chapter 2 · Rabbi Judah the Prince to Rabbi Tarfon
draftNote: The text follows the Wikisource transcription of the Kaufmann manuscript, apart from the editorial steps named in the source note; the prepared audio is being recorded; a check against the manuscript photographs is still to come. Use ⚑ correction on any mishnah to report a problem.
source: Text: the Kaufmann manuscript of the Mishnah (Budapest, Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Kaufmann A 50), fols. 169r–173v, from the diplomatic transcription on Hebrew Wikisource (כתב יד קאופמן למשנה/מסכת אבות, CC BY-SA 4.0), which records the work of the later hands. The vowel points are the manuscript's own. Where it leaves a letter of a pointed word bare, the editor has supplied the point, and the mishnah's note lists every such word; words the manuscript leaves wholly unpointed stay unpointed. Reading text: the manuscript as corrected. Letters the manuscript erases are omitted; corrections and additions by later hands, including marginal ones, are printed; marginal variant readings (נ״א) are left out. Words the scribe broke across a line end are rejoined. The scribe's abbreviations are kept, marked with a geresh (׳), and expanded in the glossary. The transcription writes Kaufmann's ḥolam, which sits over the preceding letter, as a dot on that letter; it is given here as an ordinary ḥolam. Mishnayot are numbered as in the standard printed editions; where Kaufmann divides differently, or lacks a mishnah, the note says so. Romanization: simplified, following Modern Israeli pronunciation. Pronunciation convention: Modern Israeli Hebrew applied to Kaufmann's vowels — an admitted choice, since the manuscript's pointing reflects an older Palestinian tradition. Translations made fresh from the Hebrew and Aramaic; no modern translation consulted. Audio: Google Cloud TTS, Modern Israeli Hebrew voice, reading the pointed text; abbreviations are read in full (או׳ as אוֹמֵר, שנ׳ as שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר, the divine name as Adonay).
about: Avot, "Fathers", is the tractate of the Mishnah made up of maxims; the rest of the Mishnah is law. It opens with the chain of tradition from Moses at Sinai to the Men of the Great Assembly, then gives the sayings of the sages from the early pairs down to the generation of the Mishnah's editor, Rabbi Judah the Prince. The Mishnah was compiled around 200 CE. Many communities read Avot a chapter at a time on Sabbath afternoons between Passover and Shavuot, and often through the summer, adding a sixth chapter, Kinyan Torah, to make six weeks. Chapters 1–5 here follow a single manuscript, the Kaufmann codex, probably copied in Italy in the eleventh or twelfth century and the best witness to the Mishnah's own Hebrew. It reads differently from the familiar printed text in many small places, and the notes point them out.

sentences.t: ר׳ אוֹמֵ׳ אֵי זוֹ הִיא דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה שֶׁיָּבוֹר לוֹ הָאָדָם כָּל שֶׁהִיא תִפְאֶרֶת לְעוֹשָׂה תִּפְאֶרֶת לוֹ מִן הָאָדָם וֶהֱוִוי זָהִיר בְּמִצְוָה קַלָּה כְמִצְוָה חֲמוּרָה שֶׁאֵין אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ מַתַּן שְׂכָרָן שֶׁלַּמִּצְוֹת וְהֱוֵוי מְחַשֵּׁב הֶפְסֵד מִצְוָה כְנֶגֶד שְׂכָרָהּ וּשְׂכַר עֲבֵירָה כְנֶגֶד הֶפְסֵדָהּ הִשְׂתַּכֵּל בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים וְאֵין אַתָּה בָא לִידֵי עֲבֵירָה דַּע מַה לְּמַעְלָה מִמָּךְ עַיִן רוֹאָה וְאוֹזֶן שׁוֹמַעַת וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ בְּסֵפֶר נִכְתָּבִים:
sentences.tr: Rabi omer: eizo hi derekh yeshara she-yavor lo ha-adam? Kol she-hi tif'eret le-osa, tif'eret lo min ha-adam. Ve-hevi zahir be-mitsva kala ke-mitsva ḥamura, she-ein ata yode'a matan skharan shela-mitsvot. Ve-hevei meḥashev hefsed mitsva keneged skhara, u-skhar avera keneged hefseda. Histakel bi-shlosha dvarim ve-ein ata va lidei avera: da ma le-ma'la mimakh — ayin ro'a ve-ozen shoma'at, ve-khol ma'asekha be-sefer nikhtavim.
sentences.l: Rabbi says: which is the straight path that a person should choose for himself? Any that is an honor to the one-who-does-it (and) an honor to him from people. And be careful with a light commandment as with a weighty commandment, for you do not know the giving of the reward of the commandments. And be reckoning the loss of a commandment against its reward, and the reward of a transgression against its loss. Look-closely at three things and you will not come into the hands of transgression: know what is above you — an eye seeing and an ear hearing, and all your deeds in a book are written.
sentences.i: Rabbi says: Which is the right path for a person to choose? One that does honor to the one who takes it and earns him honor from others. Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, for you do not know what reward each commandment brings. Weigh what a commandment costs you against what it earns you, and what a transgression earns you against what it costs. Keep three things in view and you will not fall into sin: know what is above you — an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book.
sentences.n: 'Rabbi' with no name is Rabbi Judah the Prince (ha-Nasi), who compiled the Mishnah around 200 CE; his son speaks in the next mishnah. הֶפְסֵד, 'loss', is what keeping a commandment costs — time, money, a pleasure given up. לִידֵי עֲבֵירָה, literally 'into the hands of transgression', is the Mishnah's ordinary way of saying 'into sin'. מִמָּךְ, 'than you', shows the Mishnaic second-person ending -akh where the Bible has -kha; you will see it constantly in this chapter (רְצוֹנָךְ, חֲבֵירָךְ, עַצְמָךְ). Kaufmann reads לְעוֹשָׂה תִּפְאֶרֶת with no 'and'; the printed editions read לְעוֹשֶׂיהָ וְתִפְאֶרֶת.
sentences.say: רַבִּי אוֹמֵר אֵי זוֹ הִיא דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה שֶׁיָּבוֹר לוֹ הָאָדָם כָּל שֶׁהִיא תִפְאֶרֶת לְעוֹשָׂה תִּפְאֶרֶת לוֹ מִן הָאָדָם וֶהֱוִוי זָהִיר בְּמִצְוָה קַלָּה כְמִצְוָה חֲמוּרָה שֶׁאֵין אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ מַתַּן שְׂכָרָן שֶׁלַּמִּצְוֹת וְהֱוֵוי מְחַשֵּׁב הֶפְסֵד מִצְוָה כְנֶגֶד שְׂכָרָהּ וּשְׂכַר עֲבֵירָה כְנֶגֶד הֶפְסֵדָהּ הִשְׂתַּכֵּל בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים וְאֵין אַתָּה בָא לִידֵי עֲבֵירָה דַּע מַה לְּמַעְלָה מִמָּךְ עַיִן רוֹאָה וְאוֹזֶן שׁוֹמַעַת וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ בְּסֵפֶר נִכְתָּבִים:

sentences.t: רַבָּ׳ גַּמְלִיאֵ׳ בְּנוֹ שֶׁלִּרְ׳ יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא אוֹ׳ יָפֶה תַלְמוּד תוֹרָה עִים דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ שֶׁיְּגִיעַת שְׁנֵיהֶם מְשַׁכְּחַת עָוֹן וְכָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁאֵין עִימָּהּ מְלָאכָה סוֹפָה בְטֵילָה לְגָרֵר עָווֹן וְכָל הָעֲמֵלִים עִים הַצִּיבּוּר יְהוּא עֲמֵלִים עִמָּהֶן לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם שֶׁזְּכוּת אֲבוֹתָם מְסַיַּיעַתָּם וְצִדְקָתָם עוֹמֶדֶת לְעַד וְאַתֶּם מַעֲלִים עֲלֵיהם שָׂכָר כְּאִילּוּ עֲשִׂיתֶם:
sentences.tr: Raban Gamliel bno shel Rabi Yehuda ha-nasi omer: yafe talmud tora im derekh erets, she-yegi'at shneihem meshakaḥat avon. Ve-khol tora she-ein ima melakha sofa vetela le-garer avon. Ve-khol ha-amelim im ha-tsibur yihyu amelim imahen le-shem shamayim, she-zkhut avotam mesaya'atam ve-tsidkatam omedet la-ad. Ve-atem — ma'alim aleihem sakhar ke-ilu asitem.
sentences.l: Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, says: fine is study of Torah with the way of the land, for the toil of both of them makes sin forgotten. And all Torah that has no work with it, its end (is to be) idle, to drag-along sin. And all who toil with the community, let them toil with them for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of their fathers helps them, and their righteousness stands forever. And you — (they) credit to-them reward as if you had done (it).
sentences.i: Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, says: Torah study goes well with a worldly occupation, for the effort both demand leaves no room for sin. All Torah study without a trade comes to nothing in the end and draws sin after it. And all who work for the community should do so for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of the community's ancestors sustains them, and their righteousness endures forever. As for you, you are credited with a reward as though you had done it all yourselves.
sentences.n: This Rabban Gamliel is Gamliel III, Rabbi Judah's son. דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, 'the way of the land', has several senses in rabbinic Hebrew; here it means earning a living. The last sentence speaks to community leaders: the good their work does is credited to them in full, though the ancestors' merit helped it along. The printed editions put it in God's mouth, מַעֲלֶה אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם שָׂכָר הַרְבֶּה, 'I credit you with a great reward'; Kaufmann has the impersonal מַעֲלִים, 'they credit', and עֲלֵיהם, 'upon them', where the sense calls for 'upon you'. The manuscript was corrected here: סוֹפָה was first written סוֹף, and a second hand changed the final pe and added the he between the lines; לְעַד וְאַתֶּם is written by a second hand over an erasure. The resh of לְגָרֵר looks like a dalet; the context and vowels show resh. יְהוּא is Kaufmann's spelling of יִהְיוּ, 'let them be', as in 1:8. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: עֲשִׂיתֶם.
sentences.say: רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל-רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא אוֹמֵר יָפֶה תַלְמוּד תוֹרָה עִים דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ שֶׁיְּגִיעַת שְׁנֵיהֶם מְשַׁכְּחַת עָוֹן וְכָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁאֵין עִימָּהּ מְלָאכָה סוֹפָה בְטֵילָה לְגָרֵר עָווֹן וְכָל הָעֲמֵלִים עִים הַצִּיבּוּר יְהוּא עֲמֵלִים עִמָּהֶן לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם שֶׁזְּכוּת אֲבוֹתָם מְסַיַּיעַתָּם וְצִדְקָתָם עוֹמֶדֶת לְעַד וְאַתֶּם מַעֲלִים עֲלֵיהם שָׂכָר כְּאִילּוּ עֲשִׂיתֶם:

sentences.t: הֱווֹן זְהִירִים בָּרְשׁוּת שֶׁאֵין מְקָרְיבִין לְאָדָם אֶלָּא לְצוֹרֶךְ עַצְמָן נִירְאִין בְּאֹהֲבִין בְּשַׁעַת הֲנָיָתָן אֵין עוֹמְדִין לְאָדָם בְּשַׁעַת דּוֹחֲקוֹ:
sentences.tr: Hevon zehirim ba-rshut, she-ein mekarvin le-adam ela le-tsorekh atsman. Nir'in be-ohavin bi-sh'at hanayatan, ein omdin le-adam bi-sh'at doḥako.
sentences.l: Be careful with the authority, for they do not bring-near a person except for the need of themselves. They appear as friends at the time of their benefit; they do not stand by a person at the time of his distress.
sentences.i: Be wary of the ruling powers: they befriend a person only for their own ends. They look like friends while it profits them, and they do not stand by a person in his hour of need.
sentences.n: Rabban Gamliel is still speaking. הָרְשׁוּת, as in 1:10, is the ruling power — in his day the Roman governors, with whom the patriarchs had to deal. הֱווֹן is a Mishnaic plural 'be!' with a final nun (printed הֱווּ). Kaufmann reads בְּאֹהֲבִין, 'in the guise of friends', where the printed editions have כְּאוֹהֲבִין, 'like friends', and it lacks the לוֹ of the printed מְקָרְבִין לוֹ לְאָדָם. The opening words are damaged in the manuscript, and the transcription prints them in brackets.

sentences.t: הוּא הָיָה אוֹ׳ עֲשֵׂה רְצוֹנוֹ כִּרְצוֹנָךְ שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה רְצוֹנָך כִּרְצוֹנוֹ בַּטֵּל רְצוֹנָךְ מִפְּנֵי רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁיְּבַטֵּל רְצוֹן אֲחֵרִים מִפְּנֵי רְצוֹנָךְ: ר׳ א׳ הֶלֵּל אוֹ׳ אַל תִּיפְרוֹשׁ מִן הַצִּיבּוּר וְאַל תַּאֲמִין בְּעַצְמָךְ עַד יוֹם מוֹתָךְ וְאַל תָּדִין אֶת חֲבֵירָךְ עַד שֶׁתַּגִּיַע לִמְקוֹמוֹ וְאַל תֹּאמַר דָּבָר שֶׁאי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהִישָּׁמַע שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לְהִישָּׁמַע וְאַל תֹּאמַ׳ כְּשֶׁאֶפָּנֶה אֶשְׁנֶה שֶׁמֵּא לֹא תִיפָּנֶה:
sentences.tr: Hu haya omer: ase retsono kirtsonakh, she-ya'ase retsonakh kirtsono. Batel retsonakh mi-pnei retsono, she-yevatel retson aḥerim mi-pnei retsonakh. Rabi omer: Helel omer: al tifrosh min ha-tsibur, ve-al ta'amin be-atsmakh ad yom motakh, ve-al tadin et ḥaverakh ad she-tagi'a li-mkomo, ve-al tomar davar she-i efshar lo le-hishama she-sofo le-hishama, ve-al tomar: kshe-epane eshne — shema lo tipane.
sentences.l: He was saying: do His will as your will, so that He will do your will as His will. Set-aside your will before His will, so that He will set-aside the will of others before your will. Rabbi says(?): Hillel says: do not separate from the community, and do not trust in yourself until the day of your death, and do not judge your fellow until you reach his place, and do not say a thing that it is impossible for it to be heard, for its end is to be heard; and do not say: when I am free I will study — lest you not be free.
sentences.i: He used to say: Do His will as though it were your own, so that He will do your will as though it were His. Set aside your will for the sake of His, so that He will set aside the will of others for the sake of yours. Hillel says: Do not cut yourself off from the community. Do not be sure of yourself until the day you die. Do not judge your fellow until you have stood in his place. Do not say anything that must never be heard, for in the end it will be heard. And do not say, 'When I have time I will study' — you may never have the time.
sentences.n: 'His will' is God's. The printed editions add כְּדֵי, 'in order that', before each שֶׁ-clause; Kaufmann's שֶׁ carries that sense on its own. With Hillel the Mishnah goes back to the sages of chapter 1, and Kaufmann starts a new mishnah at his name (the printed editions keep it all as 2:4). Before Hillel's name the manuscript has ר׳ א׳, most naturally 'Rabbi says' — a phrase out of place here, perhaps a copying slip; the printed editions have simply הִלֵּל אוֹמֵר. The clause about a thing 'impossible to be heard' is read two ways: a word that must stay private will get out in the end; or, do not speak obscurely and count on being understood eventually. The first scribe wrote שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר, 'that can be heard'; a second hand added אי, 'not'. A second hand also added the 'and' (וְ) before each of the last four sayings. אֶשְׁנֶה, 'I will study', is from שָׁנָה, 'repeat' — oral study by repetition, the root of the word Mishnah. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: תֹּאמַר, אֶפְשָׁר.
sentences.say: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר עֲשֵׂה רְצוֹנוֹ כִּרְצוֹנָךְ שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה רְצוֹנָך כִּרְצוֹנוֹ בַּטֵּל רְצוֹנָךְ מִפְּנֵי רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁיְּבַטֵּל רְצוֹן אֲחֵרִים מִפְּנֵי רְצוֹנָךְ: רַבִּי אוֹמֵר הֶלֵּל אוֹמֵר אַל תִּיפְרוֹשׁ מִן הַצִּיבּוּר וְאַל תַּאֲמִין בְּעַצְמָךְ עַד יוֹם מוֹתָךְ וְאַל תָּדִין אֶת חֲבֵירָךְ עַד שֶׁתַּגִּיַע לִמְקוֹמוֹ וְאַל תֹּאמַר דָּבָר שֶׁאי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהִישָּׁמַע שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לְהִישָּׁמַע וְאַל תֹּאמַר כְּשֶׁאֶפָּנֶה אֶשְׁנֶה שֶׁמֵּא לֹא תִיפָּנֶה:

sentences.t: הוּא הָיָה אוֹ׳ אֵין בּוּר יָרֵא חֵט וְלֹא עַם הָאָרֶץ חָסִיד וְלֹא הַבּוֹיְשָׁן לָמֵד וְלֹא הַקּוֹפְדָן מְלַמֵּד וְלֹא כָל הַמַּרְבֶּה בִסְחוֹרָה מַחְכִּים וּבִמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין אֲנָשִׁים הִשְׁתַּדֵּל לִהְיוֹת אִישׁ:
sentences.tr: Hu haya omer: ein bur yere ḥet, ve-lo am ha-arets ḥasid, ve-lo ha-boyshan lamed, ve-lo ha-kofdan melamed, ve-lo khol ha-marbe bi-sḥora maḥkim. U-vi-mkom she-ein anashim, hishtadel lihyot ish.
sentences.l: He was saying: a boor is not sin-fearing, nor a man of the land pious, nor the bashful (one) learns, nor the short-tempered (one) teaches, nor (does) everyone who does-much in trade grow-wise. And in a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.
sentences.i: He used to say: A boor cannot fear sin, and an ignorant man cannot be truly pious. The bashful do not learn, and the short-tempered cannot teach. Not everyone who spends his life in trade grows wise. And where there are no men, strive to be a man.
sentences.n: Hillel is still speaking. A בּוּר, from a word for a fallow field, is a man with no learning and no manners. עַם הָאָרֶץ, literally 'people of the land', is the Mishnah's term for someone unlearned and careless about the rabbinic rules of tithes and purity; he may mean well, but he knows too little to be pious. The bashful student never asks his question; the short-tempered teacher frightens his students into silence. אִישׁ, 'a man', is someone who takes responsibility when no one else will. חֵט is Kaufmann's spelling of חֵטְא, 'sin', without the alef, and הַבּוֹיְשָׁן (boyshan) of the printed הַבַּיְשָׁן. A second hand added the 'and' of the last two וְלֹא, the בִ of בִסְחוֹרָה, and the וּ of וּבִמְקוֹם.
sentences.say: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר אֵין בּוּר יָרֵא חֵט וְלֹא עַם הָאָרֶץ חָסִיד וְלֹא הַבּוֹיְשָׁן לָמֵד וְלֹא הַקּוֹפְדָן מְלַמֵּד וְלֹא כָל הַמַּרְבֶּה בִסְחוֹרָה מַחְכִּים וּבִמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין אֲנָשִׁים הִשְׁתַּדֵּל לִהְיוֹת אִישׁ:

sentences.t: אַף הוּא רָאָה גֻלְגֹּלֶת אָחַד צָפָה עַל פְּנֵי הַמַּיִם וְאָמַ׳ לֹהּ עַל דְּאַטִיפְתְּ אֲטִיפוּךְ בְּסוֹף מַטִּיפַייִךְ יְטוּפוּן:
sentences.tr: Af hu ra'a gulgolet aḥad tsafa al pnei ha-mayim, ve-amar lah: al de-atift atifukh, be-sof metifayikh yetufun.
sentences.l: Also he saw a skull, one, floating on the face of the water, and said to it: because you drowned, they drowned you; in the end those who drowned you will be drowned.
sentences.i: He also once saw a skull floating on the water, and said to it: Because you drowned others, you were drowned; and in the end those who drowned you will be drowned.
sentences.n: Hillel again, and in Aramaic, like his saying in 1:13. The Aramaic root טוף means 'float'; its causative means 'make float', that is, drown, and the saying turns it four times. The skull is feminine (גֻּלְגֹּלֶת), so the verbs address it as 'you (f.)'. The printed text has the feminine אַחַת, 'one'; Kaufmann writes אָחַד (aḥad). Kaufmann reads בְּסוֹף, 'in the end', where the printed text has וְסוֹף, 'and the end of'; its bet is unpointed. The transcription records a dot over the lamed of לָהּ, 'to it'. The וְ of וְאָמַ׳ was added by a second hand. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: בְּסוֹף.
sentences.say: אַף הוּא רָאָה גֻלְגֹּלֶת אָחַד צָפָה עַל פְּנֵי הַמַּיִם וְאָמַר לֹהּ עַל דְּאַטִיפְתְּ אֲטִיפוּךְ בְּסוֹף מַטִּיפַייִךְ יְטוּפוּן:

sentences.t: הוּא הָיָה אוֹ׳ מַרְבֶּה בָשָׂר מַרְבֶּה רִימָּה מַרְבֶּה נְכָסִים מַרְבֶּה דָיוֹן מַרְבֶּ׳ שְׁפָחוֹת מַרְ׳ זִימָּה מַרְבֶּ׳ עֲבָדִים מַרְבֶּ׳ גָזֵל מַרְבֶּ׳ נָשִׁים מַרְבֶּ׳ כְשָׁפִים מַרְבֶּ׳ תוֹרָה מַרְבֶּה חַיִּים קָנָה שֵׁם טוֹב קָנָה לְעַצְמוֹ קָנָה דִבְרֵי תוֹרָה קָנַ׳ חַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:
sentences.tr: Hu haya omer: marbe basar, marbe rima; marbe nekhasim, marbe dayon; marbe shfaḥot, marbe zima; marbe avadim, marbe gazel; marbe nashim, marbe khshafim; marbe tora, marbe ḥayim. Kana shem tov, kana le-atsmo; kana divrei tora, kana ḥayei ha-olam ha-ba.
sentences.l: He was saying: (who) increases flesh increases worms; increases possessions, increases [worry?]; increases maidservants, increases lewdness; increases manservants, increases robbery; increases wives, increases witchcraft; increases Torah, increases life. (Who) acquired a good name acquired (it) for himself; (who) acquired words of Torah acquired the life of the world to come.
sentences.i: He used to say: The more flesh, the more worms. The more possessions, the more worry. The more maidservants, the more lewdness; the more menservants, the more theft. The more wives, the more witchcraft. The more Torah, the more life. Whoever has gained a good name has gained it for himself; whoever has gained words of Torah has gained the life of the world to come.
sentences.n: The worms are those of the grave: a well-fed body only feeds them. Slave-women in a household were sexually available to the men of the house, slaves were reputed thieves, and rival wives were thought to resort to charms and spells. The word after 'possessions' is written over an erasure as דָיוֹן, a form found nowhere else; the printed editions have דְּאָגָה, 'worry', and the translation follows that sense. Kaufmann's list is shorter than the printed one and in a different order: the printed text puts the wives first and continues after 'more life' with study, wisdom, counsel, understanding, charity and peace. The scribe shortens מַרְבֶּה to מַרְבֶּ׳ and מַרְ׳ to fit the line. A doubled תורה and a וְ before the second קָנָה were erased. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: בָשָׂר.
sentences.say: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר מַרְבֶּה בָשָׂר מַרְבֶּה רִימָּה מַרְבֶּה נְכָסִים מַרְבֶּה דָיוֹן מַרְבֶּה שְׁפָחוֹת מַרְבֶּה זִימָּה מַרְבֶּה עֲבָדִים מַרְבֶּה גָזֵל מַרְבֶּה נָשִׁים מַרְבֶּה כְשָׁפִים מַרְבֶּה תוֹרָה מַרְבֶּה חַיִּים קָנָה שֵׁם טוֹב קָנָה לְעַצְמוֹ קָנָה דִבְרֵי תוֹרָה קָנָה חַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:

sentences.t: רַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּיִי קִיבֵּל מֵהֶלֵּל וּמִשַּׁמַּיִ הוּא הָיָה אוֹ׳ אִם עָשִׂיתָ תוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמָךְ כִּי לְכָךְ נוֹצַרְתָּ: חֲמִשָּׁה תַלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹ לְרַ׳ָ יוֹחָנָן בֵּן זַכַּיִי וְאֵילּוּ הֵן אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה ר׳ יוֹסֵף הַכֹּהֵן ור׳ שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן נְתַנְאֵל ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ הוּא הָיָה מוֹנֶה שְׁבָחָן אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס בּוֹר סוּד שֶׁאֵינוּ מְאַבֵּד טִיפָּה יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה אַשְׁרֵי יוֹלַדְתּוֹ יוֹסֵף הַכֹּהֵן חָסִיד שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן נְתַנְאֵ׳ יָרֵא חֵט אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ מַעְיָן מִתְגַּבֵּר: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵ׳ אִם יִהְיוּ כָל חַכְמֵי יִש׳ בְּכַף מֹאזְנַיִם וְאֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס בְּכַף שְׁנִייָּה מַכְרִיַע הוּא אֶת כּוּלָּם: אַבָּא שָׁאוּל או׳ מִשְּׁמוֹ אִם יִהְיוּ כָל חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵ׳ בְּכַף מֹאזְנַיִם וֶאֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס עִימָּהֶן וְאֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עַרָךְ בְּכַף שְׁנִייָּה מַכְרִיַע הוּא אֶת כּוּלָּם:
sentences.tr: Raban Yoḥanan ben Zakay kibel me-Helel u-mi-Shamay. Hu haya omer: im asita tora harbe, al taḥazik tova le-atsmakh, ki le-khakh notsarta. Ḥamisha talmidim hayu lo le-Raban Yoḥanan ben Zakay, ve-elu hen: Eli'ezer ben Horkanos, Rabi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya, Rabi Yosef ha-kohen, ve-Rabi Shimon ben Netan'el, Rabi El'azar ben Arakh. Hu haya mone shvaḥan: Eli'ezer ben Horkanos — bor sud she-einu me'abed tipa; Yehoshua ben Ḥananya — ashrei yoladto; Yosef ha-kohen — ḥasid; Shimon ben Netan'el — yere ḥet; El'azar ben Arakh — ma'yan mitgaber. Hu haya omer: im yihyu khol ḥakhmei Yisra'el be-khaf moznayim ve-Eli'ezer ben Horkanos be-khaf shniya, makhri'a hu et kulam. Aba Shaul omer mi-shmo: im yihyu khol ḥakhmei Yisra'el be-khaf moznayim, ve-Eli'ezer ben Horkanos imahen, ve-El'azar ben Arakh be-khaf shniya, makhri'a hu et kulam.
sentences.l: Rabban Yoḥanan son of Zakkai received from Hillel and from Shammai. He was saying: if you have done Torah much, do not hold goodness to yourself, for for-this you were created. Five students were his, Rabban Yoḥanan son of Zakkai's, and these are they: Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, Rabbi Joshua son of Ḥananya, Rabbi Yosef the priest, and Rabbi Simeon son of Netanel, Rabbi Elazar son of Arakh. He was counting their praise: Eliezer son of Hyrcanus — a plastered cistern that does not lose a drop; Joshua son of Ḥananya — happy is she-who-bore-him; Yosef the priest — pious; Simeon son of Netanel — fearing sin; Elazar son of Arakh — a spring growing-stronger. He was saying: if all the sages of Israel were in a pan of scales and Eliezer son of Hyrcanus in the second pan, he outweighs them all. Abba Saul says in his name: if all the sages of Israel were in a pan of scales, and Eliezer son of Hyrcanus with them, and Elazar son of Arakh in the second pan, he outweighs them all.
sentences.i: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai received the tradition from Hillel and Shammai. He used to say: If you have accomplished much Torah, take no credit for it, for this is what you were created for. Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai had five disciples: Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Rabbi Joshua ben Ḥananya, Rabbi Yosef the Priest, Rabbi Simeon ben Netanel, and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh. He used to recount their merits: Eliezer ben Hyrcanus — a plastered cistern that never loses a drop; Joshua ben Ḥananya — happy the mother who bore him; Yosef the Priest — a man of piety; Simeon ben Netanel — a man who fears sin; Elazar ben Arakh — a spring that flows ever stronger. He used to say: If all the sages of Israel were on one pan of a scale and Eliezer ben Hyrcanus on the other, he would outweigh them all. Abba Saul says in his name: If all the sages of Israel, Eliezer ben Hyrcanus among them, were on one pan of a scale and Elazar ben Arakh on the other, he would outweigh them all.
sentences.n: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai led the rabbis at Yavneh after the Romans destroyed the Temple in 70 CE. אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמָךְ, literally 'do not hold goodness to yourself', means take no credit. Kaufmann reads עָשִׂיתָ, 'done', where the printed editions have לָמַדְתָּ, 'learned'. A plastered cistern (בּוֹר, 'cistern' — compare בּוּר, 'boor', in 2:5) holds every drop poured into it: Eliezer forgot nothing he was taught. Elazar's spring makes new water of its own. The two verdicts on the scale disagree: Rabban Yoḥanan puts Eliezer first, Abba Saul puts Elazar above everyone. A second hand added in the margin לוֹ, the words יוֹחָנָן בֵּן זַכַּיִי וְאֵילּוּ הֵן, and הַכֹּהֵן; הוּא in the last line was also added in the margin. Kaufmann calls the third disciple Yosef; the printed editions have Yose (יוֹסֵי). Kaufmann starts new mishnayot at חֲמִשָּׁה תַלְמִידִים and at the second הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר; the printed editions keep it all as 2:8.
sentences.say: רַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּיִי קִיבֵּל מֵהֶלֵּל וּמִשַּׁמַּיִ הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר אִם עָשִׂיתָ תוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמָךְ כִּי לְכָךְ נוֹצַרְתָּ: חֲמִשָּׁה תַלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹ לְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֵּן זַכַּיִי וְאֵילּוּ הֵן אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה רַבִּי יוֹסֵף הַכֹּהֵן וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן נְתַנְאֵל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ הוּא הָיָה מוֹנֶה שְׁבָחָן אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס בּוֹר סוּד שֶׁאֵינוּ מְאַבֵּד טִיפָּה יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה אַשְׁרֵי יוֹלַדְתּוֹ יוֹסֵף הַכֹּהֵן חָסִיד שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן נְתַנְאֵל יָרֵא חֵט אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ מַעְיָן מִתְגַּבֵּר: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר אִם יִהְיוּ כָל חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכַף מֹאזְנַיִם וְאֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס בְּכַף שְׁנִייָּה מַכְרִיַע הוּא אֶת כּוּלָּם: אַבָּא שָׁאוּל אוֹמֵר מִשְּׁמוֹ אִם יִהְיוּ כָל חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכַף מֹאזְנַיִם וֶאֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן הוֹרְקָנוֹס עִימָּהֶן וְאֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עַרָךְ בְּכַף שְׁנִייָּה מַכְרִיַע הוּא אֶת כּוּלָּם:

sentences.t: אָמַ׳ לָהֶם צְאוּ וּרְאוּ אֵי זוֹ הִיא דֶרֶך טוֹבָה שֶׁיִּדְבַּק בָּהּ הָאָדָם ר׳ אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹ׳ עַיִן טוֹבָה ר׳ יְהוֹשֻעַ אוֹ׳ חָבֵר טוֹב ר׳ יוֹסֵה אוֹ׳ שָׁכֵן טוֹב רֶ׳ שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹ׳ הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד רֶ׳ לְעָזָר אוֹ׳ לֵב טוֹב אָמַ׳ לָהֶם רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם שֶׁבִּכְלַל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם: אָמַ׳ לָהֶם צְאוּ וּרְאוּ אֵי זוֹ הִיא דֶרֶךְ רָעָה שֶׁיִּתְרָחַק מִמֶּנָּה הָאָדָם ר׳ אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹ׳ עַיִן רָעָה ר׳ יְהוֹשֻעַ אוֹמֵ׳ חָבֵר רַע ר׳ יוֹסֵף אוֹ׳ שָׁכֵן רַע ר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹ׳ הַלֹּוֶוה וְאֵינוּ מְשַׁלֵּם אֶחָד לֹווֶה מִן הָאָדָם כְּלוֹוֶה מִן הַמָּקוֹם שנ׳ לוֹוֶה רָשָׁע וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר אוֹ׳ לֵב רַע אָמַ׳ לָהֶם רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם שֶׁבִּכְלַל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם:
sentences.tr: Amar lahem: tse'u u-re'u eizo hi derekh tova she-yidbak ba ha-adam. Rabi Eli'ezer omer: ayin tova. Rabi Yehoshua omer: ḥaver tov. Rabi Yose omer: shakhen tov. Rabi Shimon omer: ha-ro'e et ha-nolad. Rabi Le'azar omer: lev tov. Amar lahem: ro'e ani et divrei El'azar ben Arakh mi-divreikhem, she-bikhlal dvarav divreikhem. Amar lahem: tse'u u-re'u eizo hi derekh ra'a she-yitraḥek mimena ha-adam. Rabi Eli'ezer omer: ayin ra'a. Rabi Yehoshua omer: ḥaver ra. Rabi Yosef omer: shakhen ra. Rabi Shimon omer: ha-love ve-einu meshalem; eḥad love min ha-adam ke-love min ha-Makom, she-ne'emar: love rasha ve-lo yeshalem, ve-tsadik ḥonen ve-noten. Rabi El'azar omer: lev ra. Amar lahem: ro'e ani et divrei El'azar ben Arakh mi-divreikhem, she-bikhlal dvarav divreikhem.
sentences.l: He said to them: go out and see which is a good path that a person should cling to. Rabbi Eliezer says: a good eye. Rabbi Joshua says: a good companion. Rabbi Yose says: a good neighbor. Rabbi Simeon says: the one who sees the (thing) being-born. Rabbi Le'azar says: a good heart. He said to them: I see the words of Elazar son of Arakh over your words, for in the whole of his words (are) your words. He said to them: go out and see which is a bad path that a person should keep-far from. Rabbi Eliezer says: a bad eye. Rabbi Joshua says: a bad companion. Rabbi Yosef says: a bad neighbor. Rabbi Simeon says: the one who borrows and does not repay; the same (is) one-who-borrows from a person as one-who-borrows from the Omnipresent, as it is said: the wicked borrows and will not repay, and the righteous is gracious and gives. Rabbi Elazar says: a bad heart. He said to them: I see the words of Elazar son of Arakh over your words, for in the whole of his words (are) your words.
sentences.i: He said to them: Go out and see which is the good path a person should hold fast to. Rabbi Eliezer says: A generous eye. Rabbi Joshua says: A good companion. Rabbi Yose says: A good neighbor. Rabbi Simeon says: Foreseeing what will come of things. Rabbi Le'azar says: A good heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arakh to yours, for his words include yours. He said to them: Go out and see which is the bad path a person should keep away from. Rabbi Eliezer says: A grudging eye. Rabbi Joshua says: A bad companion. Rabbi Yosef says: A bad neighbor. Rabbi Simeon says: Borrowing and not repaying — borrowing from a person is the same as borrowing from the Omnipresent, as it is said, 'The wicked man borrows and does not pay back, while the righteous one shows favor and gives' (Psalms 37:21). Rabbi Elazar says: A bad heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arakh to yours, for his words include yours.
sentences.n: A 'good eye' is generosity and goodwill toward others; a 'bad eye' is envy and stinginess. הַנּוֹלָד, 'what is being born', means the consequences of what one does. הַמָּקוֹם, literally 'the Place', is a rabbinic name for God: 'the Omnipresent'. The rabbis read the verse's 'righteous one who shows favor and gives' as God, who repays the lender when the borrower defaults — so the defaulter has in effect borrowed from God. A good heart covers the other four: a man's heart produces the eye, the friendships, the neighborliness and the foresight. Kaufmann reads דֶּרֶךְ טוֹבָה, 'a good path', where the printed editions have דֶּרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה, 'a straight path', echoing 2:1. The third disciple is Yose in the first round and Yosef in the second; לְעָזָר (Le'azar) is the short form of Elazar common in Palestinian sources, and the vocalizer points the abbreviation רֶ׳ with segol. A second hand added the הָ of הָאָדָם in both rounds and the yod of וְאֵינוּ; an אֶת before the last דִּבְרֵיכֶם was erased in both rounds, and in the second verdict a later hand erased letters to turn the scribe's דִּבְרָיו אֱלִיעֶזֶר into דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר. Kaufmann makes each round a separate mishnah. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: שֶׁבִּכְלַל.
sentences.say: אָמַר לָהֶם צְאוּ וּרְאוּ אֵי זוֹ הִיא דֶרֶך טוֹבָה שֶׁיִּדְבַּק בָּהּ הָאָדָם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר עַיִן טוֹבָה רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻעַ אוֹמֵר חָבֵר טוֹב רַבִּי יוֹסֵה אוֹמֵר שָׁכֵן טוֹב רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד רַבִּי לְעָזָר אוֹמֵר לֵב טוֹב אָמַר לָהֶם רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם שֶׁבִּכְלַל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם: אָמַר לָהֶם צְאוּ וּרְאוּ אֵי זוֹ הִיא דֶרֶךְ רָעָה שֶׁיִּתְרָחַק מִמֶּנָּה הָאָדָם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר עַיִן רָעָה רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻעַ אוֹמֵר חָבֵר רַע רַבִּי יוֹסֵף אוֹמֵר שָׁכֵן רַע רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר הַלֹּוֶוה וְאֵינוּ מְשַׁלֵּם אֶחָד לֹווֶה מִן הָאָדָם כְּלוֹוֶה מִן הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹוֶה רָשָׁע וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר לֵב רַע אָמַר לָהֶם רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עָרָךְ מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם שֶׁבִּכְלַל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם:

sentences.t: הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים ר׳ אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹ׳ יְהִי כְבוֹד חֲבֵירָךְ חָבִיב עָלֶיךָ כְנַפְשָׁךְ וְאַל תְּהִי נוֹחַ לִכְעוֹס וְשׁוּב יוֹם אֶחָד לִפְנֵי מִיתָתָךְ וֶהֱוֵוי מִתְחַמֵּם כְּנֶגֶד אוּרָן שֶׁלַּחֲכָמִ׳ וֶהֱוֵוי זָהִיר מִגַּחַלְתָּן שֶׁלֹּא תִּכָּוֶוה שֶׁנְּשִׁיכָתָן נְשִׁיכַת שׁוּעַל וַעֲקִיצָתָן עֲקִיצַת עַקְרָב וּלְחִישָׁתָן לְחִישַׁת שָׂרָף וְכָל דִּבְרֵיהֶם כְּגַחֲלֵי אֵשׁ
sentences.tr: Hem amru shlosha dvarim. Rabi Eli'ezer omer: yehi khvod ḥaverakh ḥaviv alekha ke-nafshakh, ve-al tehi noaḥ likh'os, ve-shuv yom eḥad lifnei mitatakh. Ve-hevei mitḥamem keneged uran shela-ḥakhamim, ve-hevei zahir mi-gaḥaltan she-lo tikave, she-neshikhatan neshikhat shu'al, va-akitsatan akitsat akrav, u-leḥishatan leḥishat saraf, ve-khol divreihem ke-gaḥalei esh.
sentences.l: They said three things. Rabbi Eliezer says: let the honor of your fellow be dear to you as yourself; and do not be easy to anger; and repent one day before your death. And be warming-yourself facing the fire of the sages, and be careful of their coal, that you not be burned; for their bite is the bite of a fox, and their sting the sting of a scorpion, and their hiss the hiss of a serpent, and all their words like coals of fire.
sentences.i: They each said three things. Rabbi Eliezer says: Let your fellow's honor be as dear to you as your own self. Do not be quick to anger. Repent one day before your death. Warm yourself at the fire of the sages, but beware of their glowing coals, or you will be burned: their bite is a fox's bite, their sting a scorpion's sting, their hiss a serpent's hiss, and all their words are like coals of fire.
sentences.n: 'They said three things': each of the five disciples gave three sayings, and the next mishnayot take them one at a time. 'Repent one day before your death': since no one knows the day, the rabbis explained, repent every day (Shabbat 153a). The warning about the sages' coals comes from Rabbi Eliezer, who was himself excommunicated by his colleagues in a dispute. שָׂרָף is a venomous 'burning' serpent (Numbers 21:6); לְחִישָׁה is both a hiss and a whispered charm. Kaufmann's text has כְנַפְשָׁךְ, 'as yourself'; a marginal note records the variant כְשֶׁלָּךְ, 'as your own', the reading of the printed editions. מִיתָתָךְ, 'your death', has the Mishnaic -akh again. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: תְּהִי.
sentences.say: הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר יְהִי כְבוֹד חֲבֵירָךְ חָבִיב עָלֶיךָ כְנַפְשָׁךְ וְאַל תְּהִי נוֹחַ לִכְעוֹס וְשׁוּב יוֹם אֶחָד לִפְנֵי מִיתָתָךְ וֶהֱוֵוי מִתְחַמֵּם כְּנֶגֶד אוּרָן שֶׁלַּחֲכָמִים וֶהֱוֵוי זָהִיר מִגַּחַלְתָּן שֶׁלֹּא תִּכָּוֶוה שֶׁנְּשִׁיכָתָן נְשִׁיכַת שׁוּעַל וַעֲקִיצָתָן עֲקִיצַת עַקְרָב וּלְחִישָׁתָן לְחִישַׁת שָׂרָף וְכָל דִּבְרֵיהֶם כְּגַחֲלֵי אֵשׁ

sentences.t: ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹ׳ עַיִן רָעָה וְיֶצֶר הָרַע וְשִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת מוֹצִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם:
sentences.tr: Rabi Yehoshua omer: ayin ra'a, ve-yetser ha-ra, ve-sin'at ha-briyot motsi'in et ha-adam min ha-olam.
sentences.l: Rabbi Joshua says: a bad eye, and the bad inclination, and hatred of the creatures take a person out of the world.
sentences.i: Rabbi Joshua says: A grudging eye, the evil impulse, and hatred of other people drive a person out of the world.
sentences.n: יֵצֶר הָרַע, 'the evil inclination', is the rabbinic name for the drive in every person toward selfishness and sin. שִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת can mean hating people or being hated by them; either way the man ends up alone. 'Out of the world' means to an early death. In Kaufmann this saying runs straight on from Rabbi Eliezer's without a break.
sentences.say: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר עַיִן רָעָה וְיֶצֶר הָרַע וְשִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת מוֹצִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם:

sentences.t: ר׳ יוֹסֵף או׳ יְהִי מְמוֹן חֲבֵירָךְ חָבִיב עָלֵיךָ כְשֶׁלָּךְ הַתְקֵן עַצְמָךְ לִלְמֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁאֵינָה יְרוּשָׁה לָךְ וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ יִהִיוּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם:
sentences.tr: Rabi Yosef omer: yehi memon ḥaverakh ḥaviv alekha ke-shelakh. Hatken atsmakh lilmod tora, she-eina yerusha lakh. Ve-khol ma'asekha yihiyu le-shem shamayim.
sentences.l: Rabbi Yosef says: let the money of your fellow be dear to you as your own. Prepare yourself to learn Torah, for it is not an inheritance for you. And all your deeds, let them be for the sake of Heaven.
sentences.i: Rabbi Yosef says: Let your fellow's property be as dear to you as your own. Prepare yourself to study Torah, for it does not come to you by inheritance. And let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.
sentences.n: A scholar's son inherits his father's house; his father's learning he has to earn by his own study. Kaufmann names the sage Rabbi Yosef (printed: Rabbi Yose, יוֹסֵי) and has הַתְקֵן without the printed 'and'. לָךְ was added by a second hand. Kaufmann vocalizes מְמוֹן (memon) and יִהִיוּ (yihiyu).
sentences.say: רַבִּי יוֹסֵף אוֹמֵר יְהִי מְמוֹן חֲבֵירָךְ חָבִיב עָלֵיךָ כְשֶׁלָּךְ הַתְקֵן עַצְמָךְ לִלְמֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁאֵינָה יְרוּשָׁה לָךְ וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ יִהִיוּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם:

sentences.t: ר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן או׳ הֱוֵוי זָהִיר בְּקִירְיַית שְׁמַע וּכְשֶׁאַתָּה מִתְפַּלֵּל אַל תַּעַשׂ תְּפִילָּתָךְ קְבַע אֶלָּא תַחֲנוּנִים לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם בָּ״הֻ שנ׳ כִּי חַנּוּן וְרָחוּם הוּא אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד וְאַל תְּהִי רָשָׁע בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָךְ:
sentences.tr: Rabi Shimon omer: hevei zahir be-kiryat shma. U-khshe-ata mitpalel, al ta'as tfilatakh keva, ela taḥanunim lifnei ha-Makom barukh hu, she-ne'emar: ki ḥanun ve-raḥum hu, erekh apayim ve-rav ḥesed. Ve-al tehi rasha bifnei atsmakh.
sentences.l: Rabbi Simeon says: be careful with the reading of Shema. And when you are praying, do not make your prayer fixed, but pleas before the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said: for gracious and merciful is He, long of anger and great of kindness. And do not be wicked before yourself.
sentences.i: Rabbi Simeon says: Be careful about reciting the Shema. When you pray, do not make your prayer a fixed routine; make it a plea for mercy before the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said, 'For He is gracious and merciful, long-suffering and rich in kindness' (Joel 2:13). And do not think of yourself as wicked.
sentences.n: קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע is the recitation, morning and evening, of 'Hear, O Israel' (Deuteronomy 6:4–9) and the passages that go with it; it must be said within set hours. Here קֶבַע is prayer said by rote, a duty to get through — compare 1:15, where Shammai wants Torah study to be קֶבַע, fixed. A man who writes himself off as wicked stops trying to be good. The printed editions add וּבִתְפִלָּה, 'and with prayer', after קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע and רַחֲמִים, 'mercy', before תַחֲנוּנִים, and continue the verse with וְנִחָם עַל הָרָעָה, 'and relents of evil'; Kaufmann's quotation stops at וְרַב חֶסֶד. Kaufmann spells קְרִיאַת as קִירְיַית (kiryat). בָּ״הֻ abbreviates בָּרוּךְ הוּא, 'blessed be He'.
sentences.say: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר הֱוֵוי זָהִיר בְּקִירְיַית שְׁמַע וּכְשֶׁאַתָּה מִתְפַּלֵּל אַל תַּעַשׂ תְּפִילָּתָךְ קְבַע אֶלָּא תַחֲנוּנִים לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם בָּרוּךְ-הוּא שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי חַנּוּן וְרָחוּם הוּא אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד וְאַל תְּהִי רָשָׁע בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָךְ:

sentences.t: ר׳ אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵ׳ הֱוֵוי שָׁקֵד לִלְמֹד תוֹרָה מַה שֶׁתָּשִׁיב לַאֲפִיקוֹרוֹס וְדַע לִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָמֵל וּמִי הוּא בַעַל מְלַאכְתָּךְ
sentences.tr: Rabi Eli'ezer omer: hevei shaked lilmod tora, ma she-tashiv la-apikoros, ve-da lifnei mi ata amel, u-mi hu va'al melakhtakh.
sentences.l: Rabbi Eliezer says: be diligent to learn Torah — what you shall answer to an Epicurean; and know before whom you toil, and who is the master of your work.
sentences.i: Rabbi Eliezer says: Study Torah diligently, so you will know what to answer an unbeliever. And know before whom you labor, and who your employer is.
sentences.n: אֲפִיקוֹרוֹס comes from the Greek philosopher Epicurus, who taught that the gods take no interest in human affairs; in rabbinic usage it is anyone who scoffs at the tradition and its teachers. בַּעַל מְלַאכְתָּךְ, 'the owner of your work', is the employer — God. Kaufmann names Rabbi Eliezer; the printed editions have Rabbi Elazar (ben Arakh), which gives the fifth disciple his three sayings. The printed text reads שָׁקוּד for Kaufmann's שָׁקֵד, has וְדַע before מַה שֶּׁתָּשִׁיב, and ends with 'who will pay you the wage of your labor', words Kaufmann has only in 2:16. תּוֹרָה was added in the margin. Kaufmann runs this mishnah and the next two together without a break.
sentences.say: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר הֱוֵוי שָׁקֵד לִלְמֹד תוֹרָה מַה שֶׁתָּשִׁיב לַאֲפִיקוֹרוֹס וְדַע לִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָמֵל וּמִי הוּא בַעַל מְלַאכְתָּךְ

sentences.t: ר׳ טַרְפוֹן אוֹ׳ הַיּוֹם קָצָר וְהַמְּלָאכָה מְרוּבָּה וְהַפּוֹעֲלִים עֲצֵלִים וְהַשָּׂכָר הַרְבֵּה וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת דּוֹחֵק
sentences.tr: Rabi Tarfon omer: ha-yom katsar, ve-ha-melakha meruba, ve-ha-po'alim atselim, ve-ha-sakhar harbe, u-va'al ha-bayit doḥek.
sentences.l: Rabbi Tarfon says: the day is short, and the work is much, and the laborers are lazy, and the wage is much, and the master of the house is pressing.
sentences.i: Rabbi Tarfon says: The day is short, the work is great, the laborers are lazy, the wages are high, and the master of the house is pressing.
sentences.n: Rabbi Tarfon was a priest who had seen the Temple service as a young man; he belongs to the generation after Rabban Yoḥanan's disciples. The picture is a day-laborer hired by a landowner (בַּעַל הַבַּיִת, 'master of the house'): the day is a lifetime, the work is Torah and the commandments, and the employer is God.
sentences.say: רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן אוֹמֵר הַיּוֹם קָצָר וְהַמְּלָאכָה מְרוּבָּה וְהַפּוֹעֲלִים עֲצֵלִים וְהַשָּׂכָר הַרְבֵּה וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת דּוֹחֵק

sentences.t: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמ׳ לֹא עָלֶיךָ מְלָאכָה לִגְמוֹר וְלֹא אַתָּה בֶן חוֹרִים לִיבָּטֵל אִם לָמַדְתָּה תוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה נֶאֱמָן בַּעַל מְלַאכְתָּךְ לְשַׁלֵּם לָךְ שְׂכַר פְּעוּלָּתָךְ
sentences.tr: Hu haya omer: lo alekha melakha ligmor, ve-lo ata ven ḥorim libatel. Im lamadta tora harbe, ne'eman ba'al melakhtakh le-shalem lakh skhar pe'ulatakh.
sentences.l: He was saying: not upon you (is) the work to finish, and you are not a son of free-men to be-idle. If you have learned Torah much, faithful is the master of your work to pay you the wage of your labor.
sentences.i: He used to say: The work is not yours to finish, nor are you free to walk away from it. If you have studied much Torah, your employer can be trusted to pay you the wages of your labor.
sentences.n: בֶּן חוֹרִין, 'son of free men', is a free man, the legal opposite of a slave; Kaufmann has the plural ending -im, חוֹרִים. לִיבָּטֵל is the Mishnaic infinitive without he (printed לְהִבָּטֵל). The printed text is longer: 'nor are you free to desist from it; if you have studied much Torah, they give you much reward, and your employer is faithful to pay you the wage of your labor — and know that the reward of the righteous is given in the time to come.' Kaufmann's chapter ends at פְּעוּלָּתָךְ. לָמַדְתָּה spells 'you learned' with a final he, as the Bible sometimes does. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: שְׂכַר, פְּעוּלָּתָךְ.
